profile.name: Deodhani
profile.tagline: Assamese shamanic folk dance of snake goddess worship with swords and shields.
profile.insight: Performed by women or men possessed by spiritual beings, Deodhani features dancers wielding a sword and shield in a virile war dance.
profile.profile: Deodhani is a shaman folk dance from the Indian state of Assam associated with the worship of the snake goddess Marei/Maroi. Rooted in Bodo tradition, the name translates to a woman possessed by a god, though a male shaman form also exists. Solo or group performances, typically consisting of three or four women, are accompanied by an Ojha singing Xuknoni songs or Kamrupi Bor-Dhol drums. Dancers wield a sword and shield to present a virile war dance.
profile.profile_long: Deodhani is a traditional shaman folk dance originating from the Indian state of Assam, deeply rooted in Bodo culture and associated with the worship of the snake goddess Marei/Maroi. The name is derived from two words: 'Deo', meaning God, and 'Dhani', meaning woman, literally translating to a woman possessed by a god. Alongside the female shaman tradition—where group performances generally consist of three or four women—a male shaman form is also present, known as 'Deodha-Joki' in Kamrup by the Bodo people and 'Deodhai' elsewhere in Assam. During the performance, dancers take a sword and shield to present a virile war dance depicting possession by a spiritual being. Musically, the dance is accompanied by songs sung by an Ojha, a traditional chorus leader in the Darrang district of Assam. These songs, performed by Ojapali, are known as Xuknoni in undivided Darrang district, whereas in undivided Kamrup district the performance is accompanied by Kamrupi Bor-Dhol drums.

sections.origins_and_history: Deodhani is a shaman folk dance from the Indian state of Assam, of Bodo origin. The name derives from 'Deo' (God) and 'Dhani' (woman), literally meaning a woman possessed by god. A male shaman form is also present, called 'Deodha-Joki' in Kamrup by the Bodo people and 'Deodhai' elsewhere in Assam.
sections.how_it_is_danced: It can be performed either solo or in a group, with group performances generally consisting of three or four women. Dancers take a sword and shield and present a virile war dance during the performance, depicting the dance of a shaman woman or man when possessed by a spiritual being.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is generally performed to the accompaniment of songs sung by an Ojha, a traditional chorus leader in the Darrang district of Assam. These songs sung by Ojapali are known as Xuknoni in undivided Darrang district, whereas in undivided Kamrup district it is accompanied by Kamrupi Bor-Dhol's.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance form is associated with the worship of the snake goddess Marei/Maroi, depicting possession by a spiritual being.
sections.regional_variants: Male shaman forms include 'Deodha-Joki' in Kamrup by the Bodo people and 'Deodhai' elsewhere in Assam. Songs vary by region, being Xuknoni in undivided Darrang district and accompanied by Kamrupi Bor-Dhol's in undivided Kamrup district.

profile.sacred_note: Deodhani is a shamanic ritual dance involving possession by spiritual beings and worship of the snake goddess Marei/Maroi; outsiders must respect its sacred, possession-based context.
